expansion: The lecture's own cover-test slide is built around exactly this diagnosis, showing a child photograph where "the eye on the RIGHT of the photograph is TURNED IN toward the nose... = a manifest convergent deviation — ESOTROPIA of the right-of-photograph eye" (L29, slide 11), naming the cover test as the tool used to demonstrate the manifest deviation. The cover test is the most conclusive method because it works by covering the fixing eye and objectively watching the deviating eye take up fixation (or covering one eye and watching for movement on uncovering) — a direct, observable movement-based sign of misalignment, rather than an inference from a reflected light position. The corneal light reflex test (Hirschberg) is only an estimate: it infers the angle of deviation from where a light reflex falls on the cornea, and the lecture's own critique notes the deck shows the reflex displaced on its photographs without ever performing or explaining the reflex-based measurement as a formal test (L29, slide 11), making it a rougher, indirect method compared with the movement seen on covering an eye. The pin-hole test is a visual acuity test used to determine whether reduced vision is due to a refractive error, and it has no role in detecting or measuring an ocular deviation such as esotropia (not taken from the course material). Worth's four-dot test assesses binocular single vision and fusion status (or suppression/diplopia) using red-green glasses and a four-dot target; it evaluates the sensory consequences of a squint rather than directly and conclusively demonstrating the motor deviation itself, so it is less definitive for diagnosing esotropia than the cover test (not taken from the course material). The cover test remains the most direct, conclusive clinical sign of a manifest squint like esotropia.
objective: Identify the cover test as the most conclusive clinical test for diagnosing esotropia
